title: Always-On Wake Handshake
constraints: An always-on controller talks to the PMU with a **4-phase** handshake: raise `pmu_req` to request power-off, and the PMU raises `pmu_ack` once the domain is off. Drop `pmu_req` to request power-on, and the PMU drops `pmu_ack` once the domain is back. `pmu_req` may only change when `pmu_ack == pmu_req`.

States: RUN (`pmu_req = 0`), REQ_OFF (`pmu_req = 1`, waiting for ack), SLEEP (`pmu_req = 1`, `asleep = 1`), REQ_ON (`pmu_req = 0`, waiting for ack to drop). RUN → REQ_OFF on `sleep_req && !wake_irq`. REQ_OFF → SLEEP when `pmu_ack`, or → REQ_ON if a wake arrived meanwhile. SLEEP → REQ_ON on `wake_irq`. REQ_ON → RUN when `!pmu_ack`.

Wake interrupts must never be lost. In RUN, `wake_irq` produces a one-cycle `irq_out` pulse on the next cycle. In any other state it is remembered (several merge into one) and delivered as a one-cycle `irq_out` pulse when REQ_ON → RUN happens. The trip to SLEEP itself is triggered by `sleep_req`, not by an interrupt.
`irq_out` is registered and 0 otherwise. Synchronous reset → RUN, nothing pending.
hints: A wake during REQ_OFF can't abort the request (the 4-phase protocol forbids dropping `pmu_req` before the ack), so set a `pending` flag and go straight to REQ_ON once the ack arrives.
SLEEP → REQ_ON is caused by an interrupt, so it's pending too. Deliver `irq_out` when you finally reach RUN.
Draw the handshake waveform first: req ↑, ack ↑, req ↓, ack ↓.

examples.title: round trip
examples.expected: SLEEP, then RUN with one irq_out pulse

examples.check: wake during power-down is not lost
examples.title: race
examples.input: wake_irq while REQ_OFF waits for ack
examples.expected: completes the handshake, powers straight back up, irq_out delivered
